::: {.callout-tip title="Learning objectives" icon="false"}
After this lecture (and Lab 2) you can:

1. **compute** degree, closeness, betweenness, and eigenvector centrality by hand on small graphs — and **select** the right centrality for a stated question, with a justification;
2. **derive** PageRank as the fixed point of a random surfer, run two or three power iterations by hand, and explain what damping, teleport, and *personalized* PageRank each buy you;
3. **compute** clustering coefficients and explain graphlet features as a systematic subgraph census;
4. **define** modularity against its null model, step through Louvain's local-moving phase, and explain why the Laplacian's second eigenvector splits a graph;
5. **run** one round of Weisfeiler–Leman color refinement by hand and state exactly what the WL fingerprint can and cannot distinguish;
6. **build** a feature-based classifier from all of the above — and articulate why hand-crafted features hit a ceiling that no amount of engineering lifts.
:::

## The web is a graph, and importance is a fixed point

In 1998, two Stanford graduate students looked at the web the way Zachary had looked at
his karate club: as a graph whose *structure* knew something no individual page said out
loud. Every hyperlink, they argued, is a tiny endorsement. But endorsements can't just be
counted — a link *from an important page* should count for more, which is circular:
importance defined in terms of importance.

::: {.predict}
**Commit before you look.** Page Q has **one** incoming link. Page V has **four**. Which
page should a search engine rank higher — or can't you tell yet?

::: {.predict-answer}
**You can't tell yet — and that is the entire idea.** If Q's single link comes from a
major hub while V's four come from pages nobody links to, Q outranks V. Counting links
is degree centrality; *weighting them by the linker's own importance* is the recursion
that made a search engine. The figure below shows exactly this happening on a toy web.
:::
:::

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w2-hero.html >}}

The circularity turns out to be a feature: "importance flows along links" has a unique
self-consistent solution, you can compute it by iterating a matrix product, and it is —
with refinements — what founded Google. That is today's centerpiece, and it is
**classical** graph machine learning: no training, no labels, no gradients. Pure
structure, squeezed until numbers come out.

Last week you learned to *hold* a graph. This week the graph starts talking. Everything
we extract — centralities, cluster scores, community labels, refinement colors — is a
**feature**: a number per node or per graph, computed from structure alone. Stack the
features into vectors, feed them to any classifier from your ML course, and you have
graph ML as the field practiced it for decades. At the end we will find the precise
place where this recipe stalls — which is the door the rest of the course walks through.

**Roadmap.** (1) *Who matters?* — four centralities and how to pick one. (2) PageRank:
importance as a fixed point, plus the two knobs (damping, teleport) that make it work
and the personalized variant that powers recommendations. (3) *How tight-knit?* —
triangles, clustering coefficients, graphlets. (4) *Who belongs together?* — cuts and
the Laplacian's return, then modularity and Louvain. (5) A relabeling trick from 1968
that fingerprints whole graphs — and quietly bounds what GNNs will ever see. (6) The
feature-vector recipe, and its ceiling.

::: {.callout-note title="Recap — what this lecture assumes" collapse="true"}
All from Week 1:

- The **cast graph**: nodes $A\ldots F$, edges $AB, AC, AD, BC, CE, CF, EF$, degrees $(3,2,4,1,2,2)$. It is on the board again today.
- $(\mathbf{A}^k)[u,v]$ counts length-$k$ walks ([Week 1's Proposition 1](01-why-graphs.qmd#prp-walks)) — today it counts triangles.
- The Laplacian $\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{D} - \mathbf{A}$ and its quadratic form $\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{L}\mathbf{x} = \sum_{(u,v)\in\mathcal{E}}(x_u - x_v)^2$. In Week 1's Q4 you showed that for an indicator vector this **counts cut edges** — hold that thought for §4.
- BFS gives shortest-path distances in unweighted graphs.
:::

## 1. Who matters? Four answers before you choose one

"Which node is most important?" is not a question — it is four questions wearing one
coat. Each formalization below is a
<span class="term" data-def="Centrality: any function assigning each node a score meant to capture some notion of structural importance. There are dozens; the four here (plus PageRank) cover most real use.">**centrality**</span>,
and they genuinely disagree, so the skill worth having is not computing them (machines
do that) but *matching the definition to the question being asked*.

**Degree** $d_u$ — how many connections. On the cast graph the champion is $C$ with
$d_C = 4$. Cheap, local, and surprisingly hard to beat as a baseline; but it sees only
one step.

**Closeness** — how near to everyone:
$$
c_{\text{clo}}(u) \;=\; \frac{n-1}{\sum_{v \neq u} d(u,v)},
$$
the inverse of $u$'s average distance to the rest. On the cast graph, from $C$ the
distances are $1,1,2,1,1$ (to $A,B,D,E,F$) — sum $6$, closeness $5/6 \approx 0.83$.
From $D$: $1,2,2,3,3$ — sum $11$, closeness $5/11 \approx 0.45$. If you are placing a
warehouse, a fire station, or a broadcast source, this is your question.

**Betweenness** — how often *on the way*:
$$
c_{\text{btw}}(v) \;=\; \sum_{\{s,t\},\, s \neq v \neq t} \frac{\sigma_{st}(v)}{\sigma_{st}},
$$
where $\sigma_{st}$ counts shortest $s$–$t$ paths and $\sigma_{st}(v)$ those passing
through $v$. It measures brokerage: remove a high-betweenness node and traffic reroutes
or dies. On the cast graph you can enumerate by hand: every shortest path between
$\{A,B,D\}$-side and $\{E,F\}$-side threads through $C$ — six pairs, all with a unique
shortest path — so $c_{\text{btw}}(C) = 6$; the paths from $D$ to everything except $A$
thread through $A$, giving $c_{\text{btw}}(A) = 4$; everyone else scores $0$.

**Eigenvector centrality** — important is who important people know. Score each node by
the total score of its neighbors, $x_u \propto \sum_{v \in \mathcal{N}(u)} x_v$ — in
matrix form $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \lambda\mathbf{x}$: the importance vector is the
leading eigenvector of $\mathbf{A}$, computable by repeated multiplication (power
iteration — sum your neighbors, normalize, repeat until it stops changing). This is the
recursion from the hero figure, one teleport short of PageRank.

Now stop reading definitions and *push on them* — every score below recomputes live as
you edit the graph:

{{< include ../assets/d3/w2-centrality.html >}}

The kite in the widget is a famous ten-person network built by David Krackhardt
precisely because the measures disagree on it:

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w2-centralities.html >}}

Diane has the most friends, but her friends all know each other — she reaches nobody new.
Fernando and Garth are closest to everyone. Heather has few connections, yet *every*
path to Ike and Jane crosses her: pure brokerage. And eigenvector centrality sides with
degree here — measures can agree, and when they do, that agreement is itself information
about the network.

The selection discipline, in one table:

| The question sounds like… | Reach for | Because it measures |
|---|---|---|
| "who has the most direct exposure?" | degree | raw connection count |
| "where do we place the depot / who spreads news fastest?" | closeness | average distance to all |
| "whose removal fragments the network / who brokers?" | betweenness | shortest-path traffic through a node |
| "who is influential among the influential?" | eigenvector / PageRank | recursive endorsement |

A warning that saves exam points and real projects: centrality scores are
*graph-relative*. A betweenness of $6$ means nothing across graphs of different sizes;
comparisons are only meaningful within one graph (or after normalization, which every
library offers and every paper forgets to state).

## 2. PageRank: importance as a fixed point

Eigenvector centrality has two cracks on directed graphs, and the web is very directed.
A page with no inlinks scores zero — and then contributes nothing to the pages it links
to, so zeros propagate. Worse, on a graph that is not strongly connected the leading
eigenvector can concentrate all mass in one corner and ignore the rest. Both cracks are
sealed by one story.

**The random surfer.** Imagine someone clicking links forever: at a page with $d^{\text{out}}_u$
outlinks they follow one uniformly at random. Define importance as *the fraction of time
the surfer spends at each page* in the long run — the
<span class="term" data-def="Stationary distribution: a probability vector r with M r = r — running the process one more step changes nothing. For PageRank's Google matrix it exists, is unique, and is what power iteration converges to.">**stationary distribution**</span>
of the walk. Collect the click probabilities into the **column-stochastic** matrix
$$
M_{vu} \;=\; \begin{cases} 1/d^{\text{out}}_u & \text{if } u \to v \\ 0 & \text{otherwise,}\end{cases}
$$
(column $u$ says where mass at $u$ flows). Importance must satisfy
$\mathbf{r} = M\mathbf{r}$ — a fixed point: what flows in equals what is there.

Two web-shaped pathologies break the plain walk. A **dead end** (page with no outlinks)
swallows mass — columns of zeros make $M$ sub-stochastic and $\mathbf{r} \to \mathbf{0}$.
A **spider trap** (a cycle with no exits) collects mass forever — the walk enters and
never leaves, so the trap ends up with everything. The fix is almost comically direct:
*get bored sometimes*. With probability $\beta$ follow a link; with probability
$1-\beta$ jump to a uniformly random page:
$$
\mathbf{r} \;=\; \beta M \mathbf{r} \;+\; (1-\beta)\,\tfrac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}.
$$
The damping factor $\beta$ is traditionally $0.85$ — roughly, five or six clicks before
boredom. Teleporting rescues dead ends (mass reappears everywhere) and drains spider
traps (the trap leaks $1-\beta$ of its mass per step).

::: {#prp-pagerank .proposition name="PageRank exists, is unique, and power iteration finds it"}
For any $0 < \beta < 1$ the equation above has exactly one solution with
$\mathbf{r} \ge 0$, $\sum_u r_u = 1$, and iterating
$\mathbf{r}^{(k+1)} = \beta M \mathbf{r}^{(k)} + (1-\beta)\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}$ from
any starting distribution converges to it at rate $\beta^k$.
:::

<details><summary>Proof (a contraction on the simplex — no Perron–Frobenius needed)</summary>
Let $G(\mathbf{r}) = \beta M\mathbf{r} + (1-\beta)\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}$. If
$\mathbf{r}$ is a probability vector, so is $G(\mathbf{r})$: entries are nonnegative,
and since $M$'s columns each sum to $1$, $\|M\mathbf{r}\|_1 = 1$, so
$\|G(\mathbf{r})\|_1 = \beta + (1-\beta) = 1$. For two probability vectors
$\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{s}$:
$\|G(\mathbf{r}) - G(\mathbf{s})\|_1 = \beta\,\|M(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{s})\|_1 \le \beta\,\|\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{s}\|_1$,
because multiplying by a column-stochastic matrix cannot increase the $1$-norm (each
column redistributes its entry's mass without creating any). So $G$ is a
$\beta$-contraction on a complete space; by Banach's fixed-point theorem the solution
exists, is unique, and iteration converges geometrically at rate $\beta$. This is also
why large $\beta$ means slow convergence — try it in Figure 2. $\square$
</details>

::: {#exm-pr-hand .example name="Two power iterations, by hand"}
A three-page web: $X$ links to $Y$ and $Z$; $Y$ links back to $X$; $Z$ links to $Y$.
Take $\beta = 1$ for clean fractions (no teleport — this tiny web has no dead ends).
Columns of $M$: from $X$, half to $Y$, half to $Z$; from $Y$, all to $X$; from $Z$, all
to $Y$. Start uniform, $\mathbf{r}^{(0)} = (\tfrac13, \tfrac13, \tfrac13)$:
$$
\mathbf{r}^{(1)} = \left(\tfrac13,\; \tfrac16 + \tfrac13,\; \tfrac16\right) = \left(\tfrac13, \tfrac12, \tfrac16\right),
\qquad
\mathbf{r}^{(2)} = \left(\tfrac12,\; \tfrac16+\tfrac16,\; \tfrac16\right) = \left(\tfrac12, \tfrac13, \tfrac16\right).
$$
The exact fixed point solves $x = y$, $y = \tfrac{x}{2} + z$, $z = \tfrac{x}{2}$:
$\mathbf{r} = (0.4, 0.4, 0.2)$. Notice $X$ and $Y$ tie — $Y$ has fewer inlinks but its
single inlink carries half of a big page's mass. This is the midterm's favorite
computation; practice until the update is mechanical.
:::

**Personalized PageRank.** One word in the story is load-bearing: teleport to a
*uniformly random* page. Change the teleport distribution to a single page $q$ — or a
set of pages, say *this user's* purchases — and the whole rank distribution reorganizes
around $q$'s neighborhood. That variant, **Personalized PageRank (PPR)**, is the
workhorse of graph-based recommendation ("random walks with restarts"): importance
*relative to a viewpoint*. Same theorem, same iteration, one changed vector.

Watch all of it — convergence, damping, personalization — happen:

{{< include ../assets/d3/w2-pagerank.html >}}

PageRank will return twice: in Week 3, random-walk *embeddings* replace the fixed
teleport with learned co-occurrence statistics; and in Week 11, PPR-style diffusion is
how production systems localize a GNN's computation on billion-edge graphs.

## 3. How tight-knit? Triangles, clustering, graphlets

Centralities rank single nodes. The next family of features asks about a node's
*neighborhood texture*: are my friends friends with each other?

::: {#def-clustering .definition name="Local clustering coefficient"}
For a node $u$ with degree $d_u \ge 2$,
$$
C_u \;=\; \frac{\#\{\text{edges among } \mathcal{N}(u)\}}{\binom{d_u}{2}}
\;=\; \frac{\#\{\text{triangles at } u\}}{\binom{d_u}{2}} \;\in\; [0,1].
$$
The fraction of your friend-pairs who are themselves friends.
:::

On the cast graph: $C$'s neighbors are $\{A, B, E, F\}$; among the $\binom{4}{2} = 6$
pairs, exactly two are edges ($AB$ and $EF$), so $C_C = 2/6 = 1/3$. Node $A$'s
neighbors $\{B, C, D\}$ contain one edge ($BC$): $C_A = 1/3$ as well. Social networks
run high ($0.1$–$0.6$ — friends introduce friends); the web and citation graphs run much
lower; a value near the random-graph baseline $\bar d / n$ is a warning that "community
structure" may be your imagination.

Where do triangle counts come from? You already own the tool:

::: {#prp-triangles .proposition name="The diagonal of A³ counts triangles"}
$(\mathbf{A}^3)[u,u] = 2 \times \#\{\text{triangles containing } u\}$, and
$\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{A}^3) = 6 \times \#\{\text{triangles in } G\}$.
:::

<details><summary>Proof (two lines, standing on Week 1's shoulders)</summary>
By [Week 1's walk-counting proposition](01-why-graphs.qmd#prp-walks),
$(\mathbf{A}^3)[u,u]$ counts closed walks of length 3 at $u$.
A closed 3-walk cannot repeat a vertex (it would need a self-loop), so it is exactly a
triangle at $u$ traversed in one of its 2 orientations. The trace then counts each
triangle twice at each of its 3 vertices. $\square$
</details>

**Graphlets.** Triangles are one member of a family: count *all* small subgraph shapes
— the wedge, the triangle, the 4-path, the 4-star, the square, and so on — around each
node, position by position. The resulting count vector (the *graphlet degree vector*)
is a structural fingerprint far sharper than degree: two nodes can agree on degree and
clustering yet live in completely different local architectures. The price is
combinatorial: exact counts beyond 5-node graphlets are expensive, which is one reason
the next section's *iterative* fingerprint took over. In molecular graphs, graphlet-like
counts are literal chemistry — rings and motifs are function — which is why Lab 2 aims
them at protein graphs.

## 4. Who belongs together? Cuts, spectra, and modularity

Zachary's club is back, and this time we do not know the split — we want the algorithm
to *find* it. "Community" needs a definition before it needs an algorithm, and the field
settled on two families that you will now be able to derive rather than memorize.

### 4.1 The Laplacian returns: cutting where it is cheapest

In Week 1's Q4 you computed that for an indicator vector $\mathbf{x} \in \{0,1\}^n$
marking a group $S$, the quadratic form $\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{L}\mathbf{x}$ counts the
**cut edges** between $S$ and the rest. "Find a community" ≈ "find a cut that severs few
edges" — but *minimize the cut* alone and the optimizer cheats: cutting off a single
degree-1 node severs one edge. Real objectives (RatioCut, Normalized Cut) divide by the
group sizes to force balance, and the discrete problem promptly becomes NP-hard.

The escape is one of the prettiest moves in applied math: relax $\mathbf{x}$ from
$\{0,1\}$ labels to real numbers, and the balanced-cut problem becomes an eigenvector
problem. First, a fact that makes the smallest eigenvalues of $\mathbf{L}$ meaningful:

::: {#prp-components .proposition name="Zero eigenvalues count components"}
$\mathbf{L}$ is positive semidefinite, and the multiplicity of its eigenvalue $0$
equals the number of connected components of $G$.
:::

<details><summary>Proof (the quadratic form does all the work)</summary>
PSD: $\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{L}\mathbf{x} = \sum_{(u,v)\in\mathcal{E}}(x_u - x_v)^2 \ge 0$
for every $\mathbf{x}$. A vector satisfies $\mathbf{L}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ iff
$\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{L}\mathbf{x} = 0$ (PSD makes the form's null set equal the
kernel) iff $x_u = x_v$ across every edge iff $\mathbf{x}$ is constant on each connected
component. The space of such vectors has exactly one free value per component: its
dimension is the number of components. $\square$
</details>

So on a connected graph, $0 = \lambda_1 < \lambda_2$, and the eigenvector for
$\lambda_2$ — the **Fiedler vector** — is the *smoothest possible signal that is not
constant*: it minimizes disagreement-across-edges $\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{L}\mathbf{x}$
among unit vectors orthogonal to $\mathbf{1}$ (this variational characterization is
proved in Week 6, where these eigenvectors become the graph's *frequencies*). A signal
that varies as little as possible across edges but must go somewhere has one option:
sit near one value on one well-knit region, near another value on the other, and pay
its disagreement only on the thin boundary between them. Threshold it at zero and you
have cut the graph where it is cheapest.

::: {.predict}
**Commit before you look.** One eigenvector of the karate club's Laplacian, thresholded
at zero, against the real 1977 split. Zachary's hand-built min-cut model got 33 of 34.
How many does this fully automatic spectral method get?

::: {.predict-answer}
**32 of 34.** The two misses are boundary members with ties into both camps — exactly
where a smooth signal must pass through zero. No labels, no training, no model of the
conflict: one eigenvector of a matrix you already knew.
:::
:::

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w2-fiedler.html >}}

For $k$ communities, take eigenvectors $2 \ldots k$ as $k{-}1$ coordinates per node and
run $k$-means in that space — **spectral clustering**, the version you will implement
in the lab's stretch goal.

### 4.2 Modularity: communities against a null model

Spectral methods need $k$. The other family scores a *given* partition and searches for
a good one. The naive score — fraction of edges inside communities — is broken (put
everyone in one community: score $1$). The repair is a null model:

::: {#def-modularity .definition name="Modularity"}
For a partition assigning node $u$ to community $c_u$,
$$
Q \;=\; \frac{1}{2m}\sum_{u,v}\left(\mathbf{A}[u,v] - \frac{d_u d_v}{2m}\right)\delta(c_u, c_v)
\;=\; \sum_{c}\left[\frac{e_c}{m} - \left(\frac{D_c}{2m}\right)^{\!2}\right],
$$
where $e_c$ counts edges inside community $c$ and $D_c$ sums its degrees. In words:
**edges observed inside, minus edges *expected* inside** if every edge were rewired at
random while preserving all degrees.
:::

The null model is the load-bearing wall. $d_u d_v / 2m$ is the expected number of edges
between $u$ and $v$ under degree-preserving random rewiring — so two hubs being
connected earns a community almost no credit (hubs connect to everyone), while two
low-degree nodes being connected is genuine evidence of togetherness. $Q$ ranges over
roughly $[-\tfrac12, 1)$; hand-waving calibration: real community structure typically
lands in $0.3$–$0.7$.

::: {#exm-q-hand .example name="Modularity by hand, and a lesson"}
Cast graph, $m = 7$. Partition $\{A,B,C,D\}\,|\,\{E,F\}$: internal edges
$AB, AC, AD, BC$ and $EF$ — $e$-total $5$; degree sums $10$ and $4$. So
$Q = \tfrac{5}{7} - \left(\tfrac{10}{14}\right)^2 - \left(\tfrac{4}{14}\right)^2 \approx 0.122$.
Now move $C$ across: $\{A,B,D\}\,|\,\{C,E,F\}$ — *still* $5$ internal edges
($AB, AD$; $CE, CF, EF$), but degree sums $6$ and $8$:
$Q = \tfrac{5}{7} - \left(\tfrac{6}{14}\right)^2 - \left(\tfrac{8}{14}\right)^2 \approx 0.204$.
Same cut size, better modularity — the null model rewards taking the hub $C$ out of the
group whose expected internal edges its degree was inflating. Modularity is *not* a cut
count; it is a comparison against chance.
:::

**Maximizing Q: Louvain.** Exact maximization is NP-hard; the algorithm everyone
actually runs — from the 2008 Louvain paper, one of the most-used algorithms in all of
network science — is aggressive greed in two phases. **Phase 1 (local moves):** start
with every node in its own community; sweep the nodes, moving each into the neighboring
community with the best positive $\Delta Q$, until no single move helps.
**Phase 2 (aggregation):** collapse each community into a super-node (edges become
weighted) and run phase 1 on the smaller graph. Repeat until $Q$ stops improving.

<details><summary>The ΔQ that phase 1 computes (derivation for the simplest move)</summary>
Moving an isolated node $i$ (degree $d_i$) into community $c$ changes the two terms of
$Q$'s community form: the internal-edge term gains $k_{i \to c}/m$, where $k_{i \to c}$
counts $i$'s edges into $c$, and the expected term changes by
$-\left(\tfrac{D_c + d_i}{2m}\right)^2 + \left(\tfrac{D_c}{2m}\right)^2 + \left(\tfrac{d_i}{2m}\right)^2 = -\tfrac{D_c\, d_i}{2m^2}$. So
$$
\Delta Q \;=\; \frac{k_{i \to c}}{m} \;-\; \frac{D_c\, d_i}{2m^2}:
$$
real connections in, minus expected connections in. The widget's very first move is this
formula verbatim: node 0 joining node 1's singleton community, $k_{i\to c} = 1$,
$d_i = D_c = 3$, $m = 18$, giving $\Delta Q = \tfrac{1}{18} - \tfrac{9}{648} \approx +0.042$
— check the readout. Production implementations maintain $D_c$ and $k_{i \to c}$
incrementally, which is how Louvain handles hundreds of millions of edges.
</details>

{{< include ../assets/d3/w2-louvain.html >}}

The widget's stall is not a bug in the demo — it *is* the lesson. Greedy node-moves
reach a local optimum below the planted split, and the aggregation phase exists
precisely to escape such plateaus by moving whole groups at once. One caution before
you trust any $Q$: Louvain can produce internally *disconnected* communities as moves
interact; the **Leiden** algorithm (2019, optional reading) repairs this with a
refinement step and is what you should reach for in production. `networkx` ships both.

## 5. The 1968 relabeling trick

Everything so far scores nodes. To classify whole graphs — is this molecule toxic? is
this binary malware? — you need features *per graph* that can be compared across graphs
of different sizes with no shared node identity. The tool the field converged on is a
relabeling procedure published by Boris Weisfeiler and Andrei Leman in 1968, decades
before anyone needed graph features: it was built to test
<span class="term" data-def="Graph isomorphism: a bijection between two graphs' node sets that exactly preserves edges — the graphs are 'the same drawing with different names'. No polynomial-time algorithm is known for testing it in general.">**graph isomorphism**</span>
cheaply.

**Color refinement.** Give every node the same color. Then repeat: each node's new
color is a hash of *(its color, the multiset of its neighbors' colors)* — identical
inputs, identical new color. Colors can only split, never merge, so on $n$ nodes the
process stabilizes within $n$ rounds; the final **histogram of colors** is the graph's
WL fingerprint.

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w2-wl.html >}}

Read the figure bottom-up: the hash table *is* the algorithm. Round 1 rediscovers
degree — but round 2 sees deeper. $B$, $E$, and $F$ all have degree 2 and share a color
after round 1; in round 2, $B$ splits away, because $B$'s neighbor-colors are
$\{1, 3\}$ (a degree-3 node and the hub) while $E$'s and $F$'s are $\{2, 3\}$ (the hub
and *each other's* class). The refinement sees *structure around* a node, not just its
degree: after $k$ rounds, a node's color encodes the shape of its entire $k$-hop
neighborhood.

{{< include ../assets/d3/w2-wl.html >}}

What is the fingerprint good for?

::: {#prp-wl .proposition name="WL is sound, not complete"}
If two graphs' WL color histograms differ at any round, the graphs are **not
isomorphic**. The converse fails: non-isomorphic graphs can share identical histograms
at every round — two triangles versus one hexagon is the smallest natural example.
:::

<details><summary>Proof sketch (one direction each)</summary>
Soundness: an isomorphism maps each node to a node with the same degree, the same
neighbor-degrees, and inductively the same color at every round — a bijection
preserving colors makes the histograms equal. So differing histograms forbid any
isomorphism. Incompleteness: in both ring graphs every node has exactly two neighbors,
and by induction every node has the same color as every other in *both* graphs at every
round (round $k{+}1$ hashes identical pairs everywhere). The histograms agree forever,
yet one graph is connected and the other is not — you just watched this in the widget's
second scene. $\square$
</details>

**From test to feature: the WL kernel.** Shervashidze et al. (2011 — this week's
required reading) turned the fingerprint into machine learning: run $h$ rounds,
concatenate the color histograms of all rounds into one long count vector per graph,
and let the similarity of two graphs be the inner product of their vectors. Cost
$O(hm)$ — linear in edges — while beating the combinatorially expensive graphlet
kernels on most chemistry benchmarks. For a decade this was *the* way to classify
graphs, and it is the classifier you will build for protein graphs in the lab.

File one sentence away for later: **in Week 9 we will prove that message-passing GNNs
can never distinguish two graphs that WL cannot distinguish.** The 1968 trick is not
just a feature extractor — it is the ceiling of an entire architecture class you have
not met yet. When the hexagon returns, remember it fooled us honestly today.

## 6. Features into a classifier — and the ceiling

You now hold a toolbox that turns any graph into rectangles of numbers with no learning
at all:

| level | features from today | feeds |
|---|---|---|
| node | degree, closeness, betweenness, eigenvector, PageRank/PPR, clustering coefficient, graphlet degrees, community id | logistic regression, gradient boosting |
| graph | WL histogram vector, graphlet counts, size/density/degree stats | SVM with a graph kernel, gradient boosting |

This *is* a complete ML pipeline — assemble features, fit a classical model — and Lab 2
runs it three times, with a twist you should predict now. On Cora's citation graph,
seven structural *statistics* (centralities, clustering, and friends) score a dismal
≈19% against 14% chance: a paper's topic has almost nothing to do with how *important*
or *tight-knit* it is — statistics are topic-blind. Add crude *position* features — a
one-hot of the node's Louvain community — and the same classifier jumps to ≈62%,
because under homophily, topic lives in *where you sit*. That 62% is the semester's
baseline number. And on protein graphs, WL features remain close to the state of the
art *to this day* on small datasets.

So where is the ceiling? Three places, and they are structural, not fixable by more
engineering:

1. **The features are task-blind.** Betweenness does not know you are predicting paper
   topics — and the 19% above is what that blindness costs. Whatever the task actually
   needs — position in the right cluster, some pattern of co-citation, some asymmetric
   role — either survives compression into your chosen statistics or is gone before the
   classifier ever sees data. The feature designer is the bottleneck.
2. **They ignore what nodes *say*.** Cora's papers have bags-of-words; molecules have
   atom types. Today's pipeline processes structure and features in separate universes
   (concatenation at the end is a handshake, not a marriage). The whole point of
   Weeks 6–9 is machinery where structure and attributes are computed *together*.
3. **They do not improve with data.** A hundred labeled nodes or a hundred thousand —
   degree is degree. Nothing in the pipeline gets *better* by seeing more of the task.
   The defining property of representation learning, starting next week, is that the
   features themselves are what training improves.

Hold on to the baseline numbers, though. A GNN that cannot beat "logistic regression on
seven structural features" is not a deep insight — it is a bug report, and in this
course you will treat it as one.

## Common pitfalls

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 1 · Reporting 'the' centrality" icon="false"}
There is no such thing as *the* most important node — only the most important node
*under a definition*. Deliverables that say "we ranked nodes by importance" without
naming the measure and defending the match to the question are unreviewable. Say
"betweenness, because the client asked about single points of failure."
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 2 · PageRank with β = 1 because teleport 'felt like a hack'" icon="false"}
Without teleport, dead ends leak all mass and any spider trap absorbs it: the iteration
converges to zeros or to the trap, both meaningless. The hack is the theorem: $\beta < 1$
is what makes @prp-pagerank's contraction argument work at rate $\beta$. If your ranks
are all near zero or all in one clique, check β before checking your code.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 3 · Comparing modularity across graphs, or trusting its resolution" icon="false"}
$Q$ is calibrated against *this graph's* null model: $Q = 0.42$ on one network versus
$0.38$ on another says nothing about which is 'more clustered'. And modularity has a
**resolution limit**: on large graphs it refuses to see communities below roughly
$\sqrt{2m}$ internal edges, merging small genuine groups. If small communities matter,
scan a resolution parameter or use Leiden with a different objective.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 4 · Reading equal WL fingerprints as 'same graph'" icon="false"}
@prp-wl is one-directional. Equal histograms mean "WL cannot tell them apart," not
"isomorphic" — the rings pair fails it, and chemistry is full of WL-equivalent
non-identical structures. In the other direction you are safe: different fingerprints
*prove* non-isomorphism.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 5 · A fancy feature that is degree in a costume" icon="false"}
On many graphs, eigenvector centrality, PageRank, and even betweenness correlate with
degree at $0.8{+}$. Before celebrating that your feature 'predicts', check whether
plain degree predicts the same — as a control, always run the one-feature degree
baseline. (This foreshadows a Week-9 result: several published GNN gains evaporated
against properly tuned simple baselines.)
:::

## In this week's lab

[Lab 2](../labs/lab02.qmd) turns every section into running code and one honest
measurement: compute all four centralities plus PageRank on the karate club and check
your power iteration against `networkx` to six decimals; implement clustering
coefficients via $\mathbf{A}^3$ and catch the factor of two yourself; implement
modularity and verify this lecture's pencil fractions exactly, then run Louvain and
spectral bisection on the club and score both against the real 1977 split; implement
one WL round and reproduce both verdicts (path–star: caught in one round;
triangles–hexagon: never); and close with the two-stage Cora measurement — statistics
≈19%, plus community position ≈62% — that fixes your baseline for the semester.

## Required reading

**1 · Shervashidze, Schweitzer, van Leeuwen, Mehlhorn & Borgwardt — *Weisfeiler-Lehman Graph Kernels* (JMLR 2011).** [jmlr.org/papers/v12/shervashidze11a](https://jmlr.org/papers/v12/shervashidze11a.html)

::: {.reading-annotation}
The paper that turned a 1968 isomorphism test into the decade-defining graph feature.
Read §1–3 closely: the relabeling algorithm (their Fig. 2 is our Figure 4 with more
nodes) and the kernel construction; note the $O(hm)$ complexity argument, which is the
whole game. Skim the experiments with one question: on which datasets do cheap WL
features *beat* expensive graphlet kernels? When GIN appears in Week 9, this paper is
the yardstick it is measured with.
:::

**2 · Blondel, Guillaume, Lambiotte & Lefebvre — *Fast unfolding of communities in large networks* (2008).** [arXiv:0803.0476](https://arxiv.org/abs/0803.0476)

::: {.reading-annotation}
The Louvain paper: four pages of algorithm, tens of thousands of citations. Read for
the two-phase structure you stepped through in Figure 3 and for the engineering candor
— the $\Delta Q$ bookkeeping *is* the contribution; the objective was Newman's. As you
read, keep two critiques in mind: the resolution limit (they discuss it) and the
disconnected-communities defect (they missed it; Leiden, in the optional list, is the
repair). Both critiques are exam-eligible.
:::

**Also see:** Hamilton, *GRL book*, §2.1–2.3 (graph statistics, kernels, and spectral
methods — today in 20 pages) · CS224W, "Traditional Methods for Machine Learning on
Graphs".

**Optional:** Newman, [Modularity and community structure in networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/0602124)
(PNAS 2006) — where $Q$ meets eigenvectors; elegant and short ·
Traag, Waltman & van Eck, [From Louvain to Leiden](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.08473)
(Sci. Rep. 2019) — read §2's catalogue of Louvain failure modes ·
Gleich, [PageRank beyond the Web](https://arxiv.org/abs/1407.5107) (SIAM Review 2015) —
PageRank in chemistry, biology, and sports; the survey that shows a fixed point can be
a hammer · Shervashidze et al., [Efficient graphlet kernels](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v5/shervashidze09a.html)
(AISTATS 2009) · Kriege, Johansson & Morris, [A Survey on Graph Kernels](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.11835)
(2020).

## Check your understanding

<details><summary>Q1 · Selection — An epidemiologist asks: "we can vaccinate 50 airport staff; which airports?" A city planner asks: "where should the new depot go?" A regulator asks: "which bank's failure endangers the most others?" Choose a centrality for each and defend it.</summary>
Vaccination: **betweenness** (or degree as a cheap proxy) — you want to interrupt
shortest transmission paths through broker airports. Depot: **closeness** — minimize
average distance to everywhere. Contagion: **eigenvector/PageRank-family** — a bank
matters through exposure *to other exposed banks*, recursively (regulators literally
compute variants of eigenvector centrality, e.g. DebtRank). One question, one measure,
one justification — never "we used centrality".
</details>

<details><summary>Q2 · Hand computation — On the cast graph, compute the closeness of A and the betweenness of B. One of them should surprise you slightly; say which and why.</summary>
From $A$: distances $1, 1, 1, 2, 2$ to $B, C, D, E, F$ — sum $7$, closeness
$5/7 \approx 0.71$ (second best after $C$'s $0.83$). Betweenness of $B$: every pair's
shortest paths avoid $B$ — pairs within $\{A, C\}$ are direct, and everything routes
through $A$ or $C$, so $c_{\text{btw}}(B) = 0$. The mild surprise: $B$ has degree 2,
same as $E$ and $F$, and closeness $5/8$ — well-connected by distance — yet carries
zero traffic: nearness and brokerage are different resources.
</details>

<details><summary>Q3 · PageRank — For the three-page web of the worked example (X→Y, X→Z, Y→X, Z→Y), start from r⁽⁰⁾ = (1, 0, 0) instead of uniform and run two iterations with β = 1. Compare with the lecture's trajectory and state which theorem explains what you observe.</summary>
$\mathbf{r}^{(1)} = (0, \tfrac12, \tfrac12)$ (all of $X$'s mass splits to $Y, Z$);
$\mathbf{r}^{(2)} = (\tfrac12, \tfrac12, 0)$. Different trajectory, same destination
$(0.4, 0.4, 0.2)$: @prp-pagerank guarantees a *unique* fixed point with convergence
from **any** starting distribution (with teleport, at rate $\beta^k$; here even the
plain walk converges because the graph is strongly connected and aperiodic). The
initialization-independence is exam-relevant: it is why nobody worries about
warm-starting PageRank.
</details>

<details><summary>Q4 · Modularity — Compute Q for the cast-graph partition {A,B,C}|{D}|{E,F}. Compare with the two partitions from the worked example and rank all three. What is the singleton {D} costing or earning?</summary>
Internal edges: $AB, AC, BC$ in the first group, none for $\{D\}$, $EF$ in the third —
$4$ of $7$. Degree sums: $9, 1, 4$. So
$Q = \tfrac{4}{7} - \left(\tfrac{9}{14}\right)^2 - \left(\tfrac{1}{14}\right)^2 - \left(\tfrac{4}{14}\right)^2 \approx 0.572 - 0.413 - 0.005 - 0.082 = 0.072$.
Ranking: $\{A,B,D\}|\{C,E,F\}$ ($0.204$) $>$ $\{A,B,C,D\}|\{E,F\}$ ($0.122$) $>$ this
($0.072$). The singleton earns almost nothing in the null term ($-0.005$) but *costs*
the internal edge $AD$ — a leaf node nearly always belongs with its only neighbor,
which is exactly the first kind of move Louvain's phase 1 executes.
</details>

<details><summary>Q5 · WL — Run one WL round on (a) the path A–B–C–D versus the star with center X and leaves Y,Z,W; (b) the cycle C₆ versus two disjoint triangles. For each pair: distinguished or not, and what does that prove?</summary>
(a) Path: degrees $(1,2,2,1)$ — histogram after round 1: two colors, counts
$\{2, 2\}$. Star: degrees $(3,1,1,1)$ — colors with counts $\{1, 3\}$. Histograms
differ ⇒ **not isomorphic**, proved by @prp-wl's sound direction (obvious here, but the
same certificate works when graphs have $10^6$ nodes). (b) Every node in both graphs is
degree 2 with degree-2 neighbors, forever: identical histograms at every round.
This proves *nothing* about isomorphism — and indeed they are not isomorphic
(connected vs. not). WL's verdict "same" is an abstention, not a certificate.
</details>

<details><summary>Q6 · Invariance — Why is the WL feature the histogram of colors rather than the list of colors in node order? Connect your answer to Week 1's ordering trap.</summary>
The list depends on node numbering: renumber the same graph and the list permutes,
so two storage orders of one graph would get different features — the exact failure of
Week 1's "first 100 rows of A" model. The histogram forgets order: it is invariant
under node permutation, hence a function of the graph itself. This is the course's
deepest running theme in miniature — every legitimate graph feature must be
permutation-invariant (per graph) or -equivariant (per node), and you should run this
check on any feature you ever invent.
</details>

<details><summary>Q7 · The ceiling — In the lab, seven structural statistics score ≈19% on Cora, and adding a one-hot of Louvain communities lifts the same classifier to ≈62%. A colleague concludes "so we just need better community detection". Explain what the 19→62 jump actually demonstrates, and give two structural reasons the community-feature road also plateaus.</summary>
The jump shows *which kind* of structural information carries the label signal under
homophily: **position** (which region of the graph you occupy), not **statistics**
(how central or clustered you are) — topic correlates with neighborhood, not with
importance. But the road plateaus: (1) a hard partition is a lossy, task-blind
compression of position — boundary nodes get one community id and lose their mixed
affiliations, and the partition was chosen to maximize modularity, not your accuracy;
(2) the pipeline still cannot read node attributes — Cora's words never enter, and no
structural feature conjures them. What works: *continuous, learned* position (Week 3's
embeddings — trained coordinates instead of one-hot membership), then models computing
on structure and attributes jointly (Week 6 — on Cora, that road ends near 81%).
</details>

## Where this leaves us

Today you extracted everything a graph will confess without being trained: who matters
(five ways), who clusters, who belongs together, and a fingerprint for whole graphs
that a 1968 pencil-and-paper procedure computes in linear time. You also hit the wall:
every one of these features was designed by a human who did not know your task, and
none of them improves with data.

Next week we stop designing features and start *learning* them: every node gets a
vector of free parameters, and the graph itself — through random walks that you now
understand as PageRank's cousins — trains those vectors so that nearby nodes land
nearby in space. The method arrives from an unexpected direction: a 2013 breakthrough
about *words* that graph people hijacked within a year. Bring your intuition about
random surfers; in Week 3 they learn to write.
